title: Sổ bài học M6 §1–2 — xác minh ba nguồn tham chiếu, anchor omp, và cổng trôi dữ liệu
wave: M6 wave 0 — the ledger. It precedes and feeds all fifteen live M6 work items (W1, W2, W3, W4a, W4b, W5, W6, W7, W8, W9, W10, W12a, W12b, W13, W14); W11 was dropped by the plan itself. Nothing in M6 can start until the anchors this ledger registers resolve, because every W* item opens by citing a `file:line` from §2.
one_line: Turn the §1–2 lesson ledger from a prose research artifact into a machine-checked register: re-verify every `file:line` it cites against the omp tree, mark every reference-side anchor explicitly unavailable until the three upstream repos are actually fetched and pinned, and ship a `--check` script so anchor drift turns the build red instead of silently handing Monday an engineer a line that says something else.
user_visible_effect: none — internal. No runtime, CLI, TUI, or protocol behavior changes; `bun run check:ts` stays green with byte-identical output. What changes is that M6 stops being able to cite a line that does not say what the plan claims it says. The visible effect is process-shaped: W1–W14 get a register they can trust and a script that fails loudly when it stops being trustworthy, instead of a research document whose citations are unchecked.
effort: S — roughly one engineer-day, and roughly 60% of it is writing the two data files rather than code. Concretely: ~150 lines for `scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts` (the same shape as the already-blessed `scripts/gen-clippy-bazelrc.ts --check`, which is 58 lines of comment plus logic and has no unit test), ~60 lines for the verifier's own behavior test, and the rest is transcribing the ~52 omp-side anchors verified in this session into `docs/m6/anchors.json` with a content fingerprint per anchor. The genuinely unknown cost is NOT in this estimate: pinning the three reference trees requires network access and a decision that has not been made yet (see open_questions), and if that decision goes the other way the reference half of the ledger ships marked-unavailable rather than verified, which is a smaller job, not a larger one.
risk: The single most likely way to get this wrong is treating an unresolvable reference anchor as a probably-fine one and moving on. The plan's own track record in this repo argues hard against that: of the ~52 omp-side anchors checked in this session — the half of the ledger that was actually checkable — 8 were materially stale, including two off by more than 140 lines. The reference half is the half nobody checked, and it carries citations at the same level of asserted precision. An engineer who skips the fetch and assumes correctness imports 40+ phantom line numbers into fifteen downstream work items, and the failure surfaces days later as 'the plan told me to put the deny arm before line 255 and line 255 is in the middle of a different function'. The second most likely mistake is reaching for a `bun test` file that greps implementation source for a string. AGENTS.md bans that, it would not survive a rename, and the blessed `gen-clippy-bazelrc.ts --check` precedent carries no test at all. The third is wiring the check into `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and then making the item's gate depend on that push landing — the gate must be the script's exit code, which is reproducible locally, not a shared-workflow change nobody can verify in this session.
test_contract: The observable contract: `bun scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts --check` exits 0 when every register entry with `source: "omp"` resolves to a line that still contains its recorded `contains` substring, and exits 1 naming every entry that does not — including entries whose file no longer exists. A second, weaker contract: entries with `source: "reference"` never contribute a failure, but a run that has any of them MUST print an explicit `unavailable-reference` line, so 'unchecked' can never be mistaken for 'checked'. Consumer: every one of the fifteen live M6 work items opens by citing a register entry as its starting `file:line`. If this regresses, the consumer sees an editor open on a line that does not contain the code the plan told it to modify — which is not a theoretical risk, it is the observed state of 8 of the ~52 anchors as the plan currently writes them. A second, quieter consumer: a reviewer diffing a W* PR against the ledger must be able to tell a moved anchor from an unrelated edit.
gate:
DONE when, in order:

  (a) `bun scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts --check` exits 1 and the failure list contains AT LEAST these eight, by name, because they are the plan's own stale anchors: `mcp-command-controller.ts:2209` (real: 2226), `mcp-command-controller.ts:397` (real: 399), `agent-session.ts:4432` (real: 4462), `input-controller.ts:644` (real: 588), `ci.yml:531` (real: 752), `release.ts:168` (real: 310), `executor.ts:4259` (real: 4282), `tools/index.ts:431` (real: 437). This is the item's central red and it is reproduced, not assumed: every one of the eight was confirmed stale by a real command in this session (see each entry in plan_corrections for the exact command and the real line). A checker that exits 0 on this register is broken, not passing.

  (b) After the register is corrected to the verified lines, `bun scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts --check` exits 0, with every `source: "reference"` entry still printing its `unavailable-reference` line.

  (c) `bun run check:ts` is green. Verified green in this session at HEAD 808b365 with no changes applied.

  (d) `bun test test/m6-ledger-verifier.test.ts` passes. NOTE this is NOT blocked by the missing native addon — the checker and its test touch only `Bun.file` and `node:path`, importing nothing from `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives`. Demonstrated in this session: a pure `bun test` file outside the repo ran `1 pass` with the addon absent. The blanket 'bun test reports 0 pass' caveat applies to files that transitively load the addon, not to this one.

  (e) NOT a gate: whether the three reference trees are ever fetched. That is an open question, not this item's blocker. The item is done when the reference half is marked unavailable and a human owns the decision.

  On gate_can_fail: yes, and it fails for real. Step (a) is a red that the plan's own text produces — the register as-written, populated verbatim from §2, is guaranteed to fail because the plan is demonstrably wrong about 8 of its checkable anchors. Step (b) then proves the checker is not merely always-red: correcting the 8 lines turns it green. A checker that could only ever return 1 would satisfy (a) and be useless; requiring both directions is what makes this a gate rather than a decoration.
verification:
Must pass, in this order:

  1. `bun scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts --check` — exits 1 against the plan's anchors as written (the eight named in the gate), exits 0 after the register is corrected to the verified lines.

  3. `bun test test/m6-ledger-verifier.test.ts` — passes; not addon-blocked (see gate (d)).

steps.instruction: Re-run the whole drift table before writing a line of the register — do not trust this document's numbers on Monday, they are a snapshot of HEAD 808b365. Run the twelve commands listed in `verification` and record actual output. Any anchor whose result differs from the table below means the tree moved since this spec was written: prefer the fresh output, and update this spec's plan_corrections before proceeding. Sanity-check the first one by hand: `sed -n '514,516p' packages/coding-agent/src/tools/bash.ts` must print the `criticalCommand` const, the `if (!compoundSegments && criticalCommand)` guard, and a `return` with NO `policy` field. That absent `policy` field is the whole mechanism lesson 2 is about, so confirm it with your eyes before building anything on it.

Create the register and populate the omp-side half from the drift table. For each anchor, `contains` must be a short substring unique enough on that line to detect drift but not so long it breaks on an unrelated reformat — a good default is the distinctive identifier, not the whole line. Worked examples from this session, all confirmed: `packages/coding-agent/src/tools/bash.ts` line 514 contains `CRITICAL_BASH_PATTERNS.some(pattern => pattern.test(command))`; line 545 contains `Critical pattern detected`; `packages/coding-agent/src/tools/approval.ts` line 255 contains `if (mode === "yolo")`; line 267 contains `combinedUserPolicy ?? "allow"`; `packages/tui/src/tui.ts` lines 522, 1761, 1953, 2510, 2665 are the five render call sites lesson 9 names — all five confirmed at exactly those lines; `packages/coding-agent/src/collab/guest.ts:508` and `packages/collab-web/src/lib/client.ts:324` both contain `this.#welcomed = true;`, in different packages, exactly as lesson 18 claims. Use the CORRECTED line numbers throughout; where this spec and the plan disagree, this spec is right and the difference is in plan_corrections.

Populate the reference-side half — every `codex-ref/…`, `opencode-ref/…`, and `gajae-ref/…` citation in §2 — as `source: "reference"` with the right `tree` and NO line-number verification claim. First confirm they are genuinely absent: `ls -d codex-ref opencode-ref gajae-ref` returns all three MISSING, and `git ls-files | grep -E 'codex-ref|opencode-ref|gajae-ref'` returns nothing, so they are not submodules, not vendored, and not gitignored-but-present. Roughly half of §2's citations are reference-side, which means about half of the ledger is unfalsifiable today. That is the honest state; write it down rather than quietly dropping those rows or, worse, presenting them at the same confidence as the verified omp half.

Write the §1 provenance section. For each of the three reference trees record: upstream URL, the exact command to fetch it, the commit it should be pinned to, and status `UNAVAILABLE (not fetched)`. Record the omp license findings as REPRODUCED with their line evidence (`LICENSE:1`, `LICENSE:3-5`, `package.json:5`, 16 packages declaring MIT, `deny.toml` allow-list, `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` at 22901 lines). Record the three reference license claims as UNVERIFIED-pending-fetch — the plan asserts codex is Apache-2.0, opencode MIT, gajae MIT, and this session could not read a single one of those LICENSE files. Carry forward the plan's one genuinely sharp warning, which IS about the target and IS checkable: do not open `packages/coding-agent/src/config/settings.ts:294` when looking for the approval default — that line is `const result: RawSettings = {};`. The real one is `packages/coding-agent/src/tools/settings.ts:294`, `default: "yolo",`, inside `cfgToolsApprovalMode` registered at :290. Both confirmed.

Write the checker. Read `scripts/gen-clippy-bazelrc.ts` first — match its header-comment style, its `--check` exit-code convention, and its habit of naming the exact command in the doc comment. Then implement `checkAnchor` and `main` per code_shape. Three rules that are easy to get wrong and that the gate depends on: (a) a `reference` entry must print and be counted separately from failures, so a run with zero omp-side anchors and fifty reference anchors is loudly vacuous rather than quietly green; (b) a missing file is a failure, not a skip — a deleted file is exactly the drift an engineer must be told about; (c) a line beyond end-of-file is a failure. Use `Bun.file()` and `node:path` only. No `any`, no `ReturnType<>`, no inline imports, and no `console.log` restriction applies here (this is a standalone CLI script that exits without entering the TUI) but prefer `process.stderr.write` for the failure list so stdout stays parseable.

Write the two-case test described in files_touched. Point `checkAnchor` at a temp dir you populate yourself — do NOT point it at real repo files, because a test whose result depends on production source drifting is a source-grep test wearing a costume. Case 1: write a temp file whose content does not contain the anchor's `contains`, assert `status === "drift"`. Case 2: assert a `source: "reference"` anchor yields `status === "unavailable-reference"` and is not counted as a failure. Add `afterEach` cleanup of the temp dir. Per AGENTS.md, no `mock.module()`, and `vi.restoreAllMocks()` if you spy at all (you should not need to — there is nothing to mock). Then run `bun test test/m6-ledger-verifier.test.ts` and confirm it passes; this file must NOT import anything from `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives` or it will hit the addon blocker.

Add the `check:m6-ledger` script. Do not touch `check` or `check:ts` — the gate is the script invoked directly, and coupling the repo-wide type gate to a milestone artifact would make unrelated PRs fail on M6 bookkeeping. Then optionally add the CI step next to `.github/workflows/ci.yml:752`. If you do add it, keep it as its own `run:` step and do not restructure the surrounding job — a reviewer must be able to see the one-line addition in isolation.

Close the loop: run `bun scripts/verify-m6-ledger.ts --check` and paste its output into the ledger as the recorded baseline. Then write the drift table — every anchor where the plan's line differs from the verified line — into both the ledger and the spec's own downstream notes, because W1, W3, W4b, W5, W10, W12a, W12b and W14 each cite at least one of the eight stale anchors and will otherwise be implemented against the wrong line. Finally, state the three open questions (fetch authority, artifact permanence, AGPL counsel) in the ledger as explicit unowned items so they surface on Monday rather than being discovered mid-W3.

open_questions: Where do the three reference trees come from, and who pins them? None of codex-ref, opencode-ref, gajae-ref exists in this checkout — not vendored, not a submodule, not gitignored-but-present. Roughly half of §2's citations and all of §1's license table, §5's overlap measurement, and §6's bubblewrap/LGPL finding are therefore unfalsifiable today. Until someone supplies three upstream URLs and three commit pins, the honest ledger ships them as UNAVAILABLE. This is a decision, not a blocker: the item is completable with the reference half marked unchecked, and marking it is strictly better than the current state, where they read as verified.

Is the ledger a committed artifact or an ephemeral `.lavish-wip` scratch file? This matters more than it looks. If `docs/m6/anchors.json` is committed, the checker has something stable to verify and the register rots loudly. If it lives in `.lavish-wip`, it is thrown away and W1–W14 in three weeks are citing line numbers with no drift protection at all. The plan gives no guidance. RECOMMENDATION: commit under `docs/m6/` — it is documentation of verified facts, it is small, and the whole value of the item evaporates if it is throwaway.

Does the gajae AGPL question need counsel before anyone clones that tree? §1 rates gajae 'high' risk and §6 explicitly says MuPDF/AGPL is 'NOT declared removed by their own notice' and asks for confirmation before M6 is finalized. Cloning a public repo to read it is not the same act as porting from it, and this item's ledger work is reading-only — so I do not think it blocks. But a human should confirm that distinction before W3/W5/W6 port gajae code, and before anyone adds it to CI as a fetched dependency.

Should the ledger's checker be wired into CI at all, or left as a manual `bun run check:m6-ledger`? Wiring it in (alongside ci.yml:752) is what makes drift loud for everyone; leaving it manual keeps a shared workflow file out of this diff. I lean toward wiring it, but it is a repo-convention call rather than a technical one, and the gate deliberately does not depend on it either way.
